claims.text: The initial material is as-cast HfZrTiTa0.53.
The as-cast alloy has an average grain size of approximately 10 µm.
The as-cast alloy has a compressive yield strength of 786 MPa.
The as-cast alloy has a compressive fracture strain of 13.5%.
No published tensile-elongation data are available for HfZrTiTa0.53.
Four ECAP passes at 600 °C will reduce the average grain size of HfZrTiTa0.53 to below 1 µm.
Increasing grain-boundary area will promote dislocation storage.
Increasing grain-boundary area will promote more uniform slip activity.
Enhanced dislocation storage and uniform slip will delay strain localization.
Delayed localization will enhance uniform tensile elongation without significant strength loss.
The ECAP-treated alloy will exhibit room-temperature uniform tensile elongation above 5%.
The unprocessed alloy is assumed to have uniform tensile elongation below 2%.
The ECAP-treated alloy's tensile yield strength will remain within ±10% of 786 MPa.
The ECAP-treated alloy's compressive yield strength will remain within ±10% of 786 MPa.
Fragment energy release in thin-steel-target penetration will remain within ±10% of that of as-cast HfZrTiTa0.53.
The tensile and compression predictions apply at room temperature over strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
The impact prediction applies at approximately 600 m/s projectile velocity.
The hypothesis has not been validated at elevated temperatures or at strain rates above 10^3 s^-1.
Grain-refinement effects on compressive ductility are established in similar refractory alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires yield strength to remain within 10% of baseline, but the falsification rule only rejects strength losses greater than 20%; a 10–20% loss would violate the prediction without falsifying it.

The hypothesis predicts uniform tensile elongation above 5%, whereas falsification requires elongation below 3%; results from 3% through 5% would fail the prediction but would not falsify the hypothesis.
